summary: The developer machine has the key runtime (Node 24), the documentdb MCP data-plane, Azure CLI signed-in, and a broad set of DocumentDB agent skills — enough to start building the Node.js LangChain multi‑agent sample. Several cold answers were outdated or mixed up with Cosmos DB (RU model) or other neighbours; the builder must use the DocumentDB-specific CLI/group (az documentdb mongocluster, Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters), the DocumentDB connection string formats and ports, the vCore pricing model (M‑tiers), and the integrated vector and full‑text search APIs. Missing CLI tools (azd, bicep, terraform, mongosh, dotnet) are non‑blocking for a local build but are recommended for certain workflows (IaC, manual DB inspection).
summary_points: All essential build-time tools for the sample are present: Node (v24), npm/npx, the documentdb MCP server (data‑plane), Azure CLI signed in, and the Microsoft Learn (learn) MCP server.

Multiple cold answers were incorrect/outdated — primary confusions are: the resource type (mongoClusters vs databaseAccounts), CLI group (az documentdb vs az cosmosdb), billing model (vCore compute tiers not RUs), connection string format and port (DocumentDB uses mongocluster.* host names and SRV or port 10260 for local gateway), and integrated vector/full-text search support.
Agent skills for DocumentDB (data modeling, driver, vector search, indexing, local deployment, etc.) are installed and available to guide implementation.

Missing command-line tools (azd, bicep, terraform, mongosh, dotnet) are not blockers for the sample but would make some tasks (IaC, manual verification) easier — add if you want IaC or manual DB troubleshooting.

Verdict: ready_with_gaps — you can start building now, but apply the concrete corrections in Guidance For Builder and address the information gaps about LLM provider/models and embedding dims before committing index shapes or README defaults.

tools.name: node
tools.needed_for: Run the Node.js LangChain sample code, npm scripts, npx utilities.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run the Node.js sample or use npm tooling.
tools.workaround: Install Node.js 24 from nodejs.org or use nvm to provision required runtime.

tools.name: npx / npm
tools.needed_for: Install dependencies, run seed scripts, start sample app, and optionally add MCP skills with npx.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot install or run Node-based sample scaffolding and scripts.
tools.workaround: Install Node.js (includes npm/npx) or use a container with Node pre-installed.

tools.name: az
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure resources, optional cluster or firewall checks, and to fetch cluster connection strings (az documentdb commands are available).
tools.detail: azure-cli 2.89.1 with documentdb/cosmosdb-related extensions visible in inventory
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot inspect Azure resources or run az documentdb CLI examples locally; would block optional IaC/deployment steps.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal to inspect resources or request the connection string from the cloud admin; install Azure CLI.

tools.name: documentdb MCP server (data-plane)
tools.needed_for: Inspect databases/collections, create indexes, sample documents, run explain(), and verify what the sample created on the live cluster via the agentic tooling.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server with 18 tools (list_databases, find_documents, create_index, explain_operation, etc.) — requires connection_profile "default"
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to programmatically inspect the live cluster, verify indexes and query plans, or run idempotent seed/inspect steps within the agent flow.
tools.workaround: Use az CLI and portal for management, or mongosh/manual client connections (if mongosh were installed) to check collections.

tools.name: Microsoft Learn MCP (learn_microsoft_docs_search)
tools.needed_for: Search and fetch authoritative Microsoft Learn documentation to ground cold answers and implementation choices.
tools.detail: learn_microsoft_docs_search tool available; was used to verify CLI, ARM/Bicep types, vector and search features, auth modes, pricing and engine details.
tools.impact_if_missing: Would be harder to ground facts to first‑party docs; increased risk of using outdated memory.
tools.workaround: Search docs manually in a browser (learn.microsoft.com).

tools.name: Installed DocumentDB agent skills (documentdb-*)
tools.needed_for: Domain specific guidance (driver patterns, local dev, indexing, vector-search, security, deployment recommendations) used while designing the sample.
tools.detail: Many documentdb-* skills installed: documentdb-driver, documentdb-indexing, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-local-deployment, documentdb-connection, etc.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder would lose targeted, structured guidance for DocumentDB-specific choices (index shapes, local dev settings, security patterns).
tools.workaround: Fallback to general MongoDB docs or broad Azure docs; slower and higher risk of mismatch.

tools.name: azd
tools.needed_for: Optional: azd helps template-based deploy of app infra (not required for this sample because cluster exists).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run azd-driven templates locally for app infra; not required to complete Node.js sample against an existing cluster.
tools.workaround: Use npm scripts, plain Azure CLI, or Bicep/Terraform (if available) or skip IaC steps; add azd if you plan to automate end-to-end deployment.

tools.name: bicep
tools.needed_for: Optional: produce Bicep templates for provisioning; the documentdb-azure-deployment skill prefers Bicep if provisioning is needed.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot compile or run bicep templates locally; affects optional IaC flows.
tools.workaround: Use az CLI with ARM JSON or AzAPI/Terraform; or instruct builder to run `az bicep install` as needed.

tools.name: terraform
tools.needed_for: Optional: Terraform-based IaC if sample wants to include provisioning code.
tools.impact_if_missing: Blocks Terraform-based provisioning locally; not required since run environment provides an existing cluster.
tools.workaround: Provide Bicep or az CLI examples instead, or instruct builders to install Terraform.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Developer convenience to manually inspect collections/indexes from a shell and to run quick queries for verification.
tools.impact_if_missing: Manual inspection of the cluster will rely on the documentdb MCP server or the Node.js driver; slightly less convenient.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server's find/explain tools or write a small Node.js script that uses the MongoDB driver to inspect collections.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run the local DocumentDB Gateway Docker image for local dev/test (gateway runs Mongo protocol on 10260).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run a local DocumentDB container for isolated tests; sample can run against live cluster per run environment.
tools.workaround: Use the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) as requested by the sample run environment.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: databaseAccounts. Example ARM/Bicep resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: mongoClusters (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters). Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in ARM/Bicep/Terraform for vCore DocumentDB clusters.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (templates index)
Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and historical overlap: older Cosmos DB MongoDB (RU) accounts used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; the new vCore service uses a distinct resource type (mongoClusters). The cold answer describes the older CosmosDB-style resource type.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) ARM examples (older Cosmos patterns)

confusions.build_risk: Using Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep/Terraform would deploy or attempt to manage the wrong resource type (Cosmos DB account) and not configure a DocumentDB vCore mongoClusters cluster; IaC and CLI steps would fail or create unintended resources.
improvements: Update quickstart and Bicep examples that still show Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts to include a clear note and link: 'For vCore DocumentDB clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (see templates/mongoclusters)'.
Add a deprecation / migration note on the old databaseAccounts pages explaining when to use mongoClusters vs databaseAccounts.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create ... --kind MongoDB ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb command group; commands for vCore clusters are under az documentdb mongocluster (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create, az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings). The az documentdb group is available in the Azure CLI (preview/extension may be used for some preview operations).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: az cosmosdb historically managed CosmosDB accounts (databaseAccounts) including Cosmos DB's MongoDB API; the cold answer reflects the Cosmos DB CLI group rather than the newer az documentdb mongocluster commands for vCore clusters.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb mongocluster create (cosmosdb CLI docs referencing mongocluster)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb for provisioning/inspection of a vCore cluster will confuse code and scripts; commands may target the wrong API surface or fail to find mongoClusters. Automated scripts will break or mis-target resources.
improvements: Add a prominent 'use az documentdb' note in the az cosmosdb docs and in the DocumentDB quickstarts to prevent users from using the wrong CLI group.
Document the exact az commands in the sample README (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings).

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore DocumentDB clusters use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters ARM/Bicep resource (see the mongoclusters templates). Terraform deployments may use the AzAPI provider targeting Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters or the Azure Verified Modules for Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) that reference mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (templates index)
Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (Terraform AzAPI examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The old Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) resource type and the azurerm_cosmosdb_account Terraform resource are still widely used for Cosmos DB accounts; the vCore offering uses a distinct resource type (mongoClusters) that the cold answer did not name.

confusion_sources.title: ARM/Bicep examples for Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (older Cosmos samples)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong ARM/terraform resource type in IaC will either fail to provision a vCore cluster or provision the wrong kind of Cosmos account; adoption of wrong IaC artifacts would be a blocking mistake for automated provisioning.
improvements: Add explicit examples in Bicep/Terraform quickstarts that show Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for vCore clusters and how to use AzAPI provider when Terraform is used.
Add a migration note to the databaseAccounts docs explaining when to use mongoClusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical Azure Cosmos DB MongoDB API connection string: mongodb://...@<accountName>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false... Username often 'user@accountName'.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters use MongoDB-compatible connection strings targeted at the mongocluster host names (SRV or non-SRV forms). Examples use mongodb+srv://<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000, or the portal/az documentdb commands return the correct connection string. For local gateway the DocumentDB Gateway exposes Mongo protocol on port 10260 (with TLS).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell
Private Link and connection strings (DocumentDB)
documentdb-local-deployment (gateway image and port 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer matches older Cosmos DB MongoDB API connection forms (host suffixes and port 10255) and mixes SRV vs non-SRV patterns. Azure DocumentDB vCore uses mongocluster.* host names and portal/CLI-provided connection strings; local gateway uses port 10260 not 27017 or 10255.

confusion_sources.title: Examples referencing cosmos.azure.com:10255 (Cosmos DB legacy Mongo API docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix, port, or auth options can lead to connection failures, TLS/auth mechanism mismatches, or insecure configs. Hardcoding a Cosmos DB-style connection string (10255) will fail to connect to a DocumentDB vCore cluster or local gateway.
improvements: Make the connection-string examples in the quickstarts explicit: show the SRV (`mongodb+srv://<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com`) and the local gateway example (`mongodb://localhost:10260/?tls=true`), and call out which one the user should use for production vs local.
Add a short note on the cluster connection strings page explaining differences between Cosmos (legacy) endpoint forms and the DocumentDB vCore mongocluster hostnames.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed as Azure Cosmos DB throughput (Request Units, RUs).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) uses compute tiers billed by vCores (cluster tiers such as M10, M30, M40) plus storage; it is not charged by RUs. RUs are the Cosmos DB (RU) model used by Cosmos DB API for NoSQL and Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) accounts, not by vCore DocumentDB clusters.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained (compute = cluster tiers, storage)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Request Units (RUs) are the billing model for Cosmos DB (RU-based) accounts; the cold answer conflated Cosmos DB's RU model with the vCore-based DocumentDB offering.

confusion_sources.title: Request Units in Azure Cosmos DB (RU docs)

confusions.build_risk: Choosing indexing, sharding, or runtime strategies based on RUs (e.g., tuning RU/s) would be irrelevant and could lead to wrong capacity planning and cost estimates. The sample's README or cost guidance would be misleading.
improvements: Update the pricing section of any migration or quickstart pages to state clearly: 'vCore (M tiers) + storage — not RU-based; RUs apply to Cosmos DB RU accounts'.
Add a one-liner in the quickstart and README of samples clarifying which billing model applies to the cluster the sample targets.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure AD is not supported for the MongoDB wire protocol in Cosmos DB; use MongoDB-style SCRAM auth and account keys.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both NativeAuth (native username/password) and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC token) authentication for the MongoDB-compatible clusters. Admins enable MicrosoftEntraID in the cluster's authConfig and clients can use OIDC tokens or the MONGODB-OIDC / MONGODB-OIDC authMechanism in connection strings as documented.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
Connect using Microsoft Entra ID in Visual Studio Code (MONGODB-OIDC example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically, Cosmos DB's Mongo API did not support Entra ID in the same way and documentation differs across API flavors; the cold answer reflects older Cosmos constraints.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB docs that emphasize account keys for Mongo API

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only native auth is possible, they may hardcode passwords or miss the option to use managed identities/service principals for production authentication, reducing security and operational ergonomics.
improvements: Add a short how-to snippet in the quickstart showing enabling MicrosoftEntraID with az documentdb mongocluster update and a connection string example using MONGODB-OIDC.
Add a note to the auth documentation that Microsoft Entra ID support is available and how it maps to MongoDB OIDC authMechanism.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For data-plane operations use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., mongodb npm package). There is no special DocumentDB-specific data-plane driver.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. Use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., the official mongodb npm package) for data-plane operations to Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters; only control‑plane (management) tasks use Azure management SDKs or az CLI.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: The Cosmos DB MongoDB API does not expose native vector index types; a createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }) would fail.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB includes integrated vector indexes (vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, vector-diskann) and supports creating them via db.runCommand({ createIndexes: '<coll>', indexes: [{ key: { '<vecPath>': 'cosmosSearch' }, cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-hnsw'|'vector-ivf'|'vector-diskann', dimensions: <dim>, ... } }] }); searches are done via $search with the cosmosSearch operator.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector search examples)
Example creating IVF/HNSW/DiskANN vector indexes

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described historic limitations of Cosmos DB's Mongo API or assumed 'no native vector indexes' (common for some Mongo API services). The DocumentDB vCore product integrates vector search natively and exposes createIndexes/cosmosSearch options.

confusion_sources.title: Pages that describe Cosmos DB not having native vector indexes or recommending Azure Cognitive Search

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes no native vector support, they may implement an external vector DB or Azure Cognitive Search pipeline, adding complexity and duplication; they'd also configure wrong index shapes vs the integrated options.
improvements: Update any 'no native vector index' docs that are still live and conflicting to point to the DocumentDB vector-search docs with examples of createIndexes/cosmosSearch usage.
Add a clear example in the quickstart showing how to create a vector index and run a $search vector query.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Azure Cognitive Search (external index) or export documents; no built-in rich text search equivalent to MongoDB Atlas Search.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides an integrated full-text search engine using createSearchIndexes (BM25) and $search aggregate stage; hybrid search (BM25 + vector) is explicitly supported (two indexes over the same collection and Reciprocal Rank Fusion or server-side fusion via $unionWith). No external Azure Cognitive Search is required for integrated BM25 or hybrid retrieval.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes and $search overview)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many examples historically recommended Azure Cognitive Search as the external search engine for Cosmos DB; the cold answer repeats that pattern while DocumentDB vCore now includes an integrated BM25 search engine and hybrid fusion primitives.

confusion_sources.title: Older guidance recommending Azure Cognitive Search for search scenarios

confusions.build_risk: Using an external search service instead of the integrated search adds complexity, cost, and potential sync overhead; sample would be more complicated than necessary.
improvements: Add a short 'When to use external Azure Cognitive Search vs integrated DocumentDB search' note in the search docs clarifying that integrated BM25 + vector hybrid is supported and recommended for same-cluster workloads.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Assumed compatibility up to MongoDB 4.x/5.0, many features missing; uncertain.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and implements the majority of MongoDB operators (documented compatibility). Some administrative or very new server-side commands may differ; run the migration compatibility assessment for exact operator coverage.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (MongoDB compatibility and supported wire protocol versions)
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged due to historical fragmentation across API versions; it reflected older compatibility limits instead of the current v5-8 wire protocol coverage of DocumentDB vCore.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API compatibility pages showing earlier supported versions

confusions.build_risk: Assuming the wrong wire protocol may cause the builder to pin an incompatible driver version or avoid using newer aggregation operators that DocumentDB supports, reducing feature quality or causing runtime errors.
improvements: Add a short compatibility table in the quickstart and README that states explicitly the supported MongoDB wire protocol versions (5.0–8.0) and points to the compatibility matrix for operator-level details.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a local MongoDB Docker image (mongo:6.0) on port 27017; Cosmos DB emulator limited for Mongo API.
confusions.grounded_answer: For DocumentDB development use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260; the local gateway requires TLS (self-signed cert) and SCRAM-SHA-256 for auth and offers env vars SKIP_INIT_DATA / INIT_DATA_PATH for seed control.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment (Gateway image and port 10260)
Local Deployment & Developer Workflow — Azure DocumentDB (gateway image and TLS guidance)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the generic MongoDB server for local dev because that's common; DocumentDB provides a Gateway Docker image optimized for parity (port 10260, TLS) and local workflows.

confusion_sources.title: Generic advice to run mongo:6.0 locally for MongoDB-compatible development

confusions.build_risk: Using a plain mongo:6 container for local dev may hide DocumentDB-specific behaviors (vector/indexing or full-text features and port/TLS differences), resulting in integration tests that pass locally but fail on the real DocumentDB cluster.
improvements: Add a clear 'local dev' section in the quickstart that suggests the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image and shows example docker-compose with port 10260 and TLS flags.
Add a short recommended pattern: use the gateway image for DocumentDB parity; use mongo:6 only for driver-level unit tests that don't exercise DocumentDB features.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically MongoDB change streams were not fully supported; use Cosmos change feed or polling.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB change streams; change streams are supported and used by the migration tooling for online migrations. The service also provides its own change-stream/change-feed docs and examples. No separate special enablement beyond normal cluster config is required for the supported change stream usage, but for migrations you must ensure the source supports change streams and retention windows.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Migrate using online change streams (migration docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Change stream support differed across older Cosmos DB API versions and some emulators; the cold answer reflected older limitations.

confusion_sources.title: Change feed for Cosmos DB Core API (different API)

confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams are unavailable would push the builder to implement polling or an external sync approach, increasing complexity and latency, and making migration demos less realistic.
improvements: Clarify in migration quickstarts that DocumentDB supports MongoDB change streams and show a minimal code example of opening a change stream with the Node.js driver.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect a service-specific MCP server named 'documentdb' to provide data-plane inspection tools; the general Azure MCP server may not include documentdb-specific utilities.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. The documentdb MCP server exists and provides data-plane tools (list_databases, find_documents, create_index, explain_operation, etc.). The general Azure MCP server (azure) provides control-plane operations and documentation search; for data-plane inspection use the documentdb MCP server with connection_profile 'default'.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's managed JSON document database service; it was rebranded into Azure Cosmos DB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong/context-mixing: The new Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) was previously named 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and was rebranded to Azure DocumentDB as a distinct offering. This new DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine. Separately, the original 'Azure DocumentDB' (2014–2017) was an earlier product that became Azure Cosmos DB — so the same phrase has multiple historical uses; DocumentDB (current) is not the same as the original 2014 DocumentDB that became Cosmos DB.

grounding_links.title: How Azure DocumentDB relates to Azure Cosmos DB (naming and history)
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming and history)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The product naming history contains reused names: the original 'DocumentDB' (2014) later became Cosmos DB, while a more recent 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' was renamed to 'Azure DocumentDB' (new). The cold answer conflated the lineage.

confusion_sources.title: FAQ note explaining the rename from vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong historical name in docs or scripts (or instructing users to use Cosmos DB management screens) can confuse readers and induce use of the wrong APIs/CLI commands.
improvements: Add a short 'Naming history' paragraph to the top-level docs clarifying: (a) original DocumentDB -> Cosmos DB; (b) 'Azure DocumentDB' (current) was previously 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and is now a distinct, vCore-based service.
Avoid reusing 'DocumentDB' without the 'with MongoDB compatibility' suffix in any new developer-facing samples to reduce ambiguity.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The underlying engine is Cosmos DB's proprietary distributed storage and query engine that implements the MongoDB wire protocol.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect. The vCore Azure DocumentDB service is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) which is built on PostgreSQL (pg_documentdb components). It implements the MongoDB wire protocol for compatibility; application code generally uses standard MongoDB drivers and should work, but there are some service-specific operator differences documented in the compatibility matrix.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB
What is Azure DocumentDB? (engine overview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Cosmos DB's proprietary engine or older perceptions that the cloud service uses an internal engine; the current vCore product is explicitly built on the open-source DocumentDB engine — the names and engines differ across products.

confusion_sources.title: Pages implying Cosmos DB's engine is different or proprietary

confusions.build_risk: Assuming the underlying engine is MongoDB or proprietary Cosmos internals may cause a builder to expect unsupported admin commands or mis-handle operator differences. But for application-level code using standard drivers, behavior is largely compatible.
improvements: Document in the top-level overview that DocumentDB (vCore) is an open-source engine built on PostgreSQL and link to the GitHub project for transparency.
Add a 'what changes for your code' checklist showing where behaviour differs (admin commands, rare operators) and link to the compatibility matrix.

confusions.question: How will embeddings be stored and (if supported) indexed for semantic matching?
confusions.cold_answer: Store embeddings as JSON arrays of floats in 'embedding' and create vector index if supported; else external DB or in-app ANN.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct approach: store embedding as number[] and create a DocumentDB vector index using cosmosSearchOptions (kind vector-ivf/hnsw/diskann) when cluster supports vector indexes; otherwise fallback to external vector store or application-side nearest neighbour. The vector-search docs specifically require embedding: number[] and show createIndexes examples.

grounding_links.title: Vector index examples and requirements (vectors must be number[])

information_gaps.title: LLM provider & model selection
information_gaps.description: The prompt and installed skills do not specify which LLM provider or exact model names (chat + embedding) the sample should use. The builder must choose provider env vars (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, etc.), model names, and how to read them from .env. Searched installed skills and Microsoft docs; no authoritative default provided.

information_gaps.title: Embedding dimensionality and default vector index parameters
information_gaps.description: No definitive embedding dimension is supplied (the vector index parameters depend on embedding size). The vector-search docs provide limits and options but the sample must pick a concrete embedding model/dim and vector-index params (dims, kind, numLists/m/efConstruction). Looked in vector-search docs and prompt review; decision left to implementer.

information_gaps.title: Seed data exact contents and idempotency
information_gaps.description: Prompt-review suggests a seed script but no sample dataset is included. The builder needs exact sample documents (non-PHI) and idempotent seeding rules. I checked documentdb-local-deployment for sample-data guidance but found no ready seed file for this sample.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) for vCore clusters; in Azure CLI use 'az documentdb mongocluster ...' and in Bicep/ARM/Terraform target 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters'.

Read the cluster connection string from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and use the standard MongoDB driver; for local dev use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image and port 10260 (with TLS); do not hardcode cosmos.azure.com:10255-style strings.

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Plan capacity based on vCore tiers (M10, M30, M40, ... ) and storage, not RUs; document cost guidance in the sample README accordingly.

sources.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained (compute = cluster tiers)

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the integrated search and vector APIs: createSearchIndexes + $search for BM25 full-text, and createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions for vector indexes (vector-ivf/hnsw/diskann) rather than requiring Azure Cognitive Search for hybrid retrieval.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample because the run environment says the cluster already exists. Add azd only if you want template-driven app+infra demos; install via package manager (Microsoft installer or npm-based azd installer).

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Useful if you want to include Bicep IaC for cluster provisioning or to ship a Bicep template in the repo. Install via 'az bicep install' or follow the Bicep installation docs.

references.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Add Terraform only if you intend to provide Terraform examples; use the AzAPI provider to target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters. Install terraform if you will automate provisioning in CI.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh for convenience when manually debugging queries, inspecting indexes and running quick project-level checks. Install from mongodb.com or use npx mongosh.

references.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Only needed if you plan to add .NET flavors of the sample; otherwise Node.js is sufficient. If needed, install .NET SDK from Microsoft.
